stimulus.text: Historians disagree about the Great Awakening and the Revolution. Some argue the revivals trained ordinary people to defy established authority and gave distant colonies a shared experience across regions. Others note that the fires of revival had died decades before 1776, and that many patriot leaders had never been awakened.
stimulus.source_note: Background from the books and the lesson script: the historian's debate over the Awakening and the Revolution, as framed in Barron's Chapter 4.

source: original; stimulus is a summary of the books' accounts
stem: Why do historians disagree about whether the Awakening caused the Revolution?

options.text: That no records of the revivals survive for historians to study today at all.
options.misconception: Records of the revivals survive in abundance — sermons, diaries, and newspapers — so the disagreement is not about missing evidence.

options.text: That the revivals took place entirely after independence finally came in the year 1776.
options.misconception: The revivals came in the 1730s and 1740s, decades before independence, not after it.

options.text: That the Great Awakening and the Revolution happened in the very same year together.
options.misconception: The two events were separated by decades: the revivals peaked in the 1740s, independence came in 1776.

options.text: That the revivals had faded before 1776, and many patriot leaders were never awakened.

rationales.general:
1. See the two cases. One side sees defiance learned in church; the other sees a cold trail.
2. Ask what the skeptics point to. Fires dead for decades, and patriot leaders who never felt the revival.
3. Ask why that matters. A cause that fades thirty years before its effect is hard to prove.
4. Name the disagreement. It is about whether a shared habit can outlive the revival that taught it.
Remember: the debate is live because the evidence pulls both ways — a trained habit of defiance, and a trail gone cold by 1776.
rationales.D: The disagreement turns on timing and on who was actually awakened. The revival fires had died decades before 1776, and many patriot leaders had never experienced a conversion — so the link from revival to Revolution is hard to prove, even though the revivals did teach ordinary people to judge authority for themselves. Background: historians still argue the question because both sides have real evidence, and no document settles it. The other options misstate the basic facts of when the revivals happened.
rationales.A: Records of the revivals survive in abundance — sermons, diaries, and newspapers — so the disagreement is not about missing evidence.
rationales.B: The revivals came in the 1730s and 1740s, decades before independence, not after it.
rationales.C: The two events were separated by decades: the revivals peaked in the 1740s, independence came in 1776.
